en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Having thoroughly examined the Atharvaveda as well as the Kaumārī Saṃhitā, the rule for the fulfillment of desires was correctly composed by Buddhirāja.
Or rather, as in the *Āñchākalpalatā-uddhāra*, according to the *Prayogapārijāta* in the *Atharvaṇa*: Maheśvara said,
"One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) at the fourth watch, at midnight, even without the solar disc."

The meditation on the Goddess is as previously described. One should meditate upon the Vidyā of the fourth peak (kūṭa), which has the luster of a ruby, consists of thirteen syllables, and is like a thousand-petaled lotus, within the nostril; then, one should [visualize] the Tāraka outside.

Having invoked [the deity] from the maṇḍala, one should meditate upon the Goddess born from that supreme space (paramākāśa), possessing the form previously described. Then, while uttering the fourth *kūṭa*, one should offer the *arghya* water;
with this very [mantra], one should satisfy her three times. One should conquer [the obstacles] by reciting the *turīya-gāyatrī*.
Having first performed the *nyāsa* and other preliminary rites, one should recite the root-vidyā of Kālanityā one hundred and eight times;
having recited the fourth *kūṭa* that same number of times, one should offer it,
and after praising her, [one should contemplate her] as she ascends into the supreme space within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.

One should likewise meditate upon the Self as consisting of the Kāmakalā. This fourfold twilight rite (saṃdhyācatuṣṭaya) is mandatory for those who worship this Vidyā, but it is not proclaimed for other mantras. When external [rituals] are impossible, the twilight rite consists of meditation.

The worship is prescribed for the night; having prepared it, the Vidyā is proclaimed as follows: *tāra* (the syllable Om), *vāc* (the goddess of speech), *śrī* (prosperity), *māyā* (the seed-syllable Hrīm), *dya* (the sky), *kāma* (desire), *varāhakam*—meaning the name *varāhaka*, which is *glauṃ*, the seed-mantra of Gaṇeśa—and *gu* (the earth), *ruṃ*.

Then follows the fifteen-syllable mantra: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, which is said to be the triad of seeds (*bīja*) pertaining to Tripura. Subsequently, in conjunction with what precedes it, it is said to consist of twenty-nine syllables;
thus, through these two modes of conjunction, it is recited in all four variations.

Whatever *ṛc*s there are, whatever *yajuṣ* there may be, one should recite those six in direct order; then one should recite those same six again in reverse order, excluding the sixth. In this way, there are eleven *ṛc*s, including the two *anuṣaṅgas*.
Then, for the sake of swift propitiation, one should recite the mantra for Gaṇapati;

thereafter, one should recite the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) preceded by the *dvāradā* (the syllable *hūṃ*). Then one should recite: "Bring all people under my control, svāhā! Following that, there should be the seed-syllables *sauṃḥ*, *klīṃ*, and *aim*.
This subsequent [verse] is a supplement (anuṣaṅga) to the Goddess; this [supplement] consists of thirty-six syllables.

By means of the preceding and subsequent supplements, one should recite eleven verses (*ṛc*). By this, it is stated that there are indeed eleven verses in the supplements. Nevertheless, in the mantras beginning with "Tāra" (Oṃ), [one should place] Bālā...

The meaning is that because the fire will be described later in the passage beginning with "the sprouting of a young girl," the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "by connection with the preceding and following [verses]" indicates that one should also join the twelfth verse with the preceding and following verses. [One should recite] the *gāyatrī*... and so forth.

The verses beginning with "Tryambakaṃ," "Jātavedase," and "Samāno mantraḥ" occurred in reverse order; however, for each turn (paryāya), one should recite the sixth verse, which is "Bhittvā bhittvā," "Saṃbhindhi yavasa," and "Saṃgacchadhvam. [The verse] "Samāno mantraḥ... [is used].
Having recited the eleventh verse beginning with *trastārtīyasamānīva*, one should then recite the twelfth verse.
Thus, there would be twelve verses—both distinct and non-distinct—across all four sections (*paryāya*). [The verses are: *gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ* and *agnim īḷe*. *mṛtyumataḥ*.
Next: "He who has grasped me"—this is for the third [verse]. "We have conquered today"—this is for the fourth.
First, the *vyāhṛtis* are recited; then the mantra beginning with "Bhadraṃ naḥ. Then, in the first [part], "Bhadraṃ no marutām ojasā"; then in the third, "Indro viśvasya... and so on.
One should then recite: "teṣāṃ no bhavatu" (may it be for us), followed by "oṃ hrīṃ vaṃ ṭhaṃ amṛta rudrāya".

Then, having spoken of the noose (*pāśa*), the hook (*aṅkuśa*), and so forth, [one says]: "May that which is unfavorable perish; bring that which is favorable under my control. [This is followed by] two *ṭha*s and *dama*.

If there are two *pṛg* meters with *ya*, *ta*, *na*, and *la* [in the first four feet], and thereafter the *tāra* (the fifth foot) consists of *rī*, *vaṃ*, *ṭha*, and so on, in these four [syllables] it would be equal;
the fifth, sixth, and seventh [feet] are each identical to the third. Thus ends the section known as the Kalpalatā.

This sequence for nasal administration (nasya) has been set forth; now, the procedure for bloodletting (rvaṇa) is recorded in the work titled *Prayogapārijāta*. Thus ends the "Extraction of Desires" (*Bāñchoddhāra*).

Elsewhere, in the Kumārasaṃhitā as well, Śrī Śiva said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the mantra known as the Wish-Fulfilling Creeper (Vāñchākalpalatā), the most wonderful secret of Gaṇanātha, which is the Śrīvidyā. First, [one should worship] the Guru..."
Having bowed to Nādhyakṣa, Kṣetrapāla, and Sarasvatī, and having uttered this mantra,
one should then perform three *tālas* (clapping of the hands), followed by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) using the root mantra,
and then pervade [the body] with it three times; thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the mantra, preceded by the [names of the] seer (*ṛṣi*) and deity (*devatā*).
Who are the sages of this collection of hymns for the mind of Gaṇeśa—who is a wish-fulfilling creeper for his devotees—which has been told by me?
The deity is Ānandabhairava; the Gaṇaka is Sarvamantravit; and [the lineage] is Āṅgirasa-Kāśyapa.
The conversation between Pañcaśiṣṭha, the best of sages, and Viśvāmitra is proclaimed as the [Pañcaśiṣṭha-]Ṛṣi;
many meters are to be known here individually,
beginning with the Devī-nivṛt, and likewise the Gāyatrī and Anuṣṭubh meters for the gods.
The *Tācamahādevī*, the illustrious *Tripurasundarī*, Gaṇeśa, Agni, and the dialogue known as *Amṛta*— along with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*) of *Śrīṃ*, *Hrīṃ*, and *Klīṃ*,
and the *kīlaka* (the pinning mantra), O Great Goddess— are employed for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goals.

The yogi is thus described; *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*), while *svāhā* is called the pin (*kīlaka*). This procedure for the distinction between the placement on the hands and the limbs (*karāṅga-nyāsa-bheda*) is now declared. Having first uttered the *Bālā* mantra, one should address the *Sundarī* in the vocative case; *hrīṃ* is released according to the sequence.
Then, O beloved, [one should worship] Māyā with the six castes enriched by the obstacles (vighnas), using the five seeds joined with long vowels in sequence:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
O Goddess of the gods, having performed the daily *ṣaḍaṅga* ritual for the Universal Self (*sarvātman*),
one should meditate upon the supreme Śrī Tripurā with the mantra "Hemādau hemapīṭhe," and likewise worship Vighneśa with the two mantras beginning with "Vījāpūra" and "Dhavala."

This meditation (dhyāna) has been declared in all the Tantras; one should meditate upon Śiva as being like a crystal, which grants the fulfillment of all desires. Having thus meditated in an auspicious place according to those distinctions, the practitioner [should perform] the meditations.

In the context of the ritual application (*prayoga*), it will be stated that one should recite [the mantra] for the sake of attaining the desired success, joined with the "acquisition of knowledge" (*vidyā-grahaṇa*). The meaning of "by its distinction" (*tad-bhedena*) is "by the distinction of Vedic mantras. "Acquisition of knowledge" means initiation (*dīkṣā*). One should recite it eight times daily.

One shall obtain whatever is desired; practitioners should always recite the mantra of Śrīvidyā, which accomplishes all aims, sixteen thousand times according to the rules for *puraścaryā*, along with the application of *tarpaṇa* and *havana*. Dharma!
One obtains wealth, desire, and union with the deity; what need is there for much speaking?
Whatever the practitioner desires, he constantly attains it all from this wish-fulfilling creeper of the mind. And according to the sequence, [it reveals] the divisions of the *Ṛgveda*...

And it has been said: for the easy understanding of practitioners and for the accomplishment of their desired goals, [the method] has been explained individually. Śrī Śiva said: O Kuleśvarī, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra in its entirety; this extraction is not to be disclosed.

For those desiring the welfare of all everywhere, [one should worship] Tāra, Vāgbhava, Ramā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Śivā, Ādyā, Kāmā, Dharaṇī, Gaṇanātha, the pair of Yakṣa-bījas, Sarit, Dīrgha, and the mantra of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī along with her daughter.
First, one should speak and converse with *numatha* and so forth; then, whatever obstacle-seed (*vighna-bīja*) may arise today,
the practitioner should conversely recite the King of Mantras (*mantra-rāja*) in sequence for the sake of swift propitiation— thus it is said regarding Gaṇapa.
One should say "Caturthyāvaravarada" (O Fourth One, Bestower of Boons), then "madamukta" (freed from intoxication).

After that, one should say "pāśa-śakti-aṅkuśaiḥ sarvajanam eva śam ānaya" (by means of the noose, spear, and goad, bring all people under my control). Then one should say the three-syllabled mantra of the Avarā Bālā ending in "svāhā," and [the mantra of] her daughter.

The meaning is that there are three seed-syllables of Bālā. One should utter the Sāvitrī mantra preceded by Tārā (Oṃ) and ending with Bālā; then one should utter the Tryambaka mantra, followed by the Jātavedas mantra, and here also the Samāna mantra.
And likewise for *dyuvaset*. Thus, having begun with the *viṅmaṃtra* class as described by the path of ascent (*ārohamārga*), one should speak the descent (*pratiroha*) starting from the same mantra;
then, the descent concludes with the verse beginning "yadadya kaccit."
One should join here either the verse "kaṃ gaṇānāṃ tvā" or the twelfth [verse]; at the end of the *pratiroha* of the Bālā, one should speak this;
then state the subsequent [verse], having first uttered the *vyāhṛti*, [and then] "bhadraṃ no api vātaya."
One should utter *praṇava*, *bhuvaneśī*, and the two *vaṃṭha* seeds;
one should utter *amṛtarudra* and the fourth, the *pāśa* seed; *hṛllekhā* and the *aṅkuśa* are declared, and then one should utter the word *pratikūla*.

One should recite the *Mamanaśyatvanukūla* mantra; then, having uttered "O Fire, bring [her] under my control" (*vaśamānaya*), one should recite the *Nala-sūkta*. Having thus chanted the *Nala-sūkta*—which concerns both Damayantī and Nala—four times, one should proceed.

If there should be a single repetition [of the mantra], then one should recite it eight times daily, and the desired success will be attained. Likewise, one should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the Praṇava, the Tryambaka, the Jātavedasa, and the verse beginning with "saṃ samid yuvase."

In this manner, ascent (*āroha*) and descent (*avaroha*) are likewise described; that which ends with the *ṛc* "yad adya" is called the *māna-mantra*. Ascent is also said to apply to the second *dala* (petal) in the same way.
One should say "go" at the sixth [step]; the descent is the same.
Here too, in place of the twelfth [syllable], one should utter "O Agni, [ward off] wrath," and one should recite the second *vyāhṛti*, "to the vigor of the Maruts."
One should likewise state [the mantra] in the sixth position for the third leaf;
here too, one should join the *samāna* mantra in the twelfth [position],
and having recited "O Agni, protect me," one should utter [the name] ending with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess).

One should utter the third *vyāhṛti*; likewise, one should speak [the syllable] in the sixth position of the fourth *dala*. At the end of the *ṛc*, one should mutter there the triad of *vyāhṛtis* in sequence.
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should recite "Śanno bhava" for bipeds and "Catuṣpade" for quadrupeds; here too, the subsequent half-verse should be employed.
Having thus chanted four times separately for each, the most excellent practitioner—
Thus has this secret been told, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should recite it sixteen thousand times, or even six thousand times; O Goddess, one should offer oblations with milk-rice, wood-apple fruits, and sesame seeds.

One shall accomplish that which is impossible to accomplish in the world and bring even the uncontrollable under one's control; what need is there for much speaking here? One shall obtain all desires.
Thus ends the extraction of the Vāñchākalpalatā mantra from the Kumārasaṃhitā.

The Twelfth Chapter on the Glory [of the Vidyā]. Within that very interval, there is no need for the ritual of the Wish-Fulfilling Creeper (Vāñchākalpalatā), nor for fire-offerings (homa) or libations (tarpaṇa); by the mere remembrance of the Vidyā, whatever one desires shall come to pass. By a single recitation, it becomes [subservient].

By five circumambulations of Lakṣmī, the world becomes subject to one's will; by ten circumambulations, one becomes Viṣṇu; and by a hundred circumambulations, one becomes Rudra-Śakti, a sovereign of the whole earth—of this there is no doubt. In that regard, it is also stated in another [text]: "The circumambulation..."
In that regard, through five recitations, Lakṣmī brings the world under one's control;
with ten recitations, one becomes a possessor of power among the gods, such as Śiva and others;
and with one hundred thousand recitations, even a poor man becomes a sovereign emperor.

The statement of Vasiṣṭha regarding the Atharvaṇa is not a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). However, in the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the *homa* must necessarily be performed; this is according to the *Vāñchākalpalatā*, which refers to the obligatory [daily] practice. Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) in accordance with the root texts.

Having performed the fourth twilight (turīyā saṃdhyā) according to Hemādri’s injunctions regarding the visualization, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Vāñchākalpalatā* during the final watch of the night;
this is the primary time for this recitation at night.
As follows, from three *yāmas* after midnight until sunrise:
*Oṃ śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ | śrīgurubhyo namaḥ | śrīkṣetrapālāya namaḥ | Sarasvatyai namaḥ*.

Salutations to Her, the illustrious Tripurasundarī; salutations. Having recited the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), performed the three *tāla* gestures, and performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, [one should proceed] with "Oṃ Ma" for this Śrī Vāñchākalpalatā Vidyā-gaṇa...
For the collection of various hymns (*sūkta*) of the *Śasyamāna-mantra*, the sages are Ānandabhairava,
Gaṇaka, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Saṃvanana; the meters are Devīgāyatrī, Nivṛdgāyatrī, and Paṅkti.

The meters are Kṛti, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī; the deities are the nectar of the dialogue between the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, Gaṇapati, and Agastya, and Rudra; the seed-syllable (bīja) is Śrīṃ, the power (śakti) is Hrīṃ, and the heart (kīlaka) is Klīṃ.

Salutations to Lakṣmī, who stands like a wish-fulfilling creeper for the attainment of desired objects through the grace of Rudra and the nectar arising from the dialogue between the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati and Mahātripurasundarī.

Having thus resolved upon the yoga: "Obeisance to the sages Ānandabhairava, Gaṇaka, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Saṃvanana; obeisance to the head. Obeisance to the goddess Gāyatrī, the Nivṛt-chandas."
Salutations to the meters Triṣṭubh, Paṅkti, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Gāyatrī at the mouth;
salutations to the nectar of the dialogue between the illustrious Tripurasundarī and Mahāgaṇapati, and to Gaṇeśa, Amṛta, and Rudra at the heart; salutations to the Śrī-bīja.

One should place *hrīṃ* at the secret place, *śa* at the two knees, *namas* at the two feet, and *klīṃ* at the *kīlaka*; then one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra upon the *ādhāra*.
[The mantra is: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ ke ī la hrīṃ gaṇapataye*.
*Hasakalahrīṃ varavarada sakalahrīṃ sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*— thus, in the forty-third [verse],
*aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīmattripurasundarīṃ hrīṃ sarvajñāyai hrāṃ gāṃ*.
To the Brahman-self, salutation with the two thumbs; *aiṃ hrīṃ* to the eternally satisfied one, *hrīṃ gī* to the universal self, *svāhā* with the two index fingers;
*aiṃ hrīṃ* to the beginningless awareness, *hrūṃ gūṃ* to the Rudra-self, [salutation] with the two middle fingers.
*Bhyāṃ vaṣaṭ* to Aiṃ Hrīṃ Svatantrāyai Hraiṃ Gaiṃ Īśvarātmane;
to the two ring fingers, *hraṃ aiṃ hrīṃ nityamaluptāyai hrauṃ gauṃ sadāśivātmane*; to the two little fingers.

Vauṣaṭ! Aiṃ Hrīṃ! To Anantā, Hraḥ Gaḥ! To the Self of All, Phaṭ! Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other limbs, one should again pervade [the body] three times with the root mantra and meditate.
There, on a golden pedestal from the Hemādri [mountain], she was being praised by hosts of immortals;
she shone resplendent, her lotus-hands holding a flower, a noose, and a goad,
dressed in crimson and exceedingly red, with four jeweled [eyes] emerging from her in all directions.

In the final watch of the night, one should worship the Goddess, the bestower of prosperity, who is established in her own state as the single Vidyā of the five Śaktis, having been consecrated by Yakṣas and Kalaśas,
and who holds a lotus seed, a fruit, a mace, a sugarcane bow, a discus, a lotus, and a noose-lotus.

He should be meditated upon as holding in his upraised lotus-hands a grain of rice, the tip of his own tusk, and a jewel-pitcher, embraced by his beloved who holds a lotus in her hand and is adorned with blazing ornaments;
he is the one who effects the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe.
Bestowing special benefits even amidst obstacles, seated in the center of a white lotus-king and a moon, holding a supreme noose and the gestures of boon and fearlessness,
together with a goad, possessing an immortal body, the color of the moon and milk, and having three eyes.

Bow down to him who is worthy of worship by the gods, who swiftly bestows blessings, who rests upon a blossoming lotus, whose head is moistened by the nectar flowing from the crescent moon bound to his crest,
whose eyes are the moon, fire, and sun, and who holds in his hands the mudrās, the Vedas, the noose, and the rosary.
"I bow to the Lord who is as white as a garland of crystal, silver, and pearls"—
this is the meaning of the *mudrājñānamudrā*. Having thus meditated and displayed the *mudrā*, [one recites] the *Śrī Tripurasundarī-Mahāgaṇapati-Saṃvāda*.

Saying "Gaṃ, I offer the fragrance consisting of the element earth to Gaṇeśa, Amṛta, and the Rudras; obeisance," one should offer it with the little finger and the thumb. Saying "Śrīṃ, I offer the flower consisting of the element ether to the Three-eyed One (Tripura) and the Rudras; obeisance," [one should offer it].

One should offer [the incense] with the thumb and index finger, saying: "To the venerable Tripurasundarīs, I offer this incense consisting of smoke; *namaḥ*. One should offer it with the thumb and index finger, [saying]: "To the venerable Tripurasundarīs..."

Saying "I offer this lamp, whose nature is fire (raṃ), namaḥ," one should present it with the middle fingers and thumbs. Saying "To the illustrious Tripuradras, I offer this food offering (naivedya) consisting of nectar (caṃ), namaḥ," one should present it with the ring fingers and thumbs.
Saying, "Obeisance; I offer this betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), which consists of all things, to the glorious Tripuradras," one should offer it with all the fingers.
Having thus worshipped with these sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should cultivate the same state of being toward the Guru, the Deity, and the Self.
Having offered [the oblation], one should mutter slowly and gradually as follows: *oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ guṃ rī ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ soṃ*.
"Whatever it may be, O slayer of Vṛtra, you have risen up."

O Sūrya, O Sarvatadra, O Indratevaśagu, for the sake of swift propitiation, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons: Hrīṃ Kroṃ, bring all people under my control, Svāhā! Sauṃḥ Klīṃ Aiṃ Dadroṃ Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Laṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ Gu Gurīṃ.

*Keīlahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ | tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt | Yaṃ kṣipra-prasādanāya gaṇapataye vara-v.* [The mantra: *Keīlahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. [The Gāyatrī: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects. [And] to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, for the sake of swift propitiation.
rada āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ guṃ rī ke ī la hrīṃ hasaka halahrīṃ sakala hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ tryambakaṃ yaḥ.
O Jāmaheśugandhi, nourisher of prosperity,
may I be released from death as a cucumber is released from its bond; for the sake of swift propitiation, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, *hīṃ kroṃ*, bring all people under my control, svāhā!
Hā saum klīṃ aiṃ oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ guṃ rī ka e ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ jāta-vedase sunavāma somaṃ arātīyata nidaḥ pāti vedas saṃ.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties as if across a river; he protects us and leads us beyond all misfortunes.
For the sake of swift propitiation, [I offer] to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons: *hrīṃ kroṃ*, bring all people under my control, *svāhā*! *soṃ klīṃ aiṃ*. *oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ*.

*Hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ guṃ rī ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. "We have the same mantra, the same assembly, the same mind; come, their consciousness is the same; [I consecrate] this with the same mantra."

With this identical oblation, I offer to Gaṇapati, who is swift in granting grace and the bestower of boons: *trayevaḥ samānena vo haviṣā juhomi gaṃ kṣipraprasādanāya gaṇapataye varavaradāṃ hrīṃ kroṃ sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ | oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ*.

klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ guṃ rī ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ | O Agni, who art rich in fuel, in barley, and in rain, kindle all things for us; in the place of Ilā you are kindled; bring hither to us all treasures, Gaṃ!
O Gaṇapati, who quickly bestows grace, who grants boons, hrīṃ klīṃ, bring all knowledge under my control, svāhā! sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ.
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gu gurīṃ kai ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ. The mantra is equal, the assembly is equal, the mind is equal, [may we be] together.
One should consecrate their common mantra with:

Like Agni, cross over the ocean of misfortunes with the boat of the *ṛg* verses.
O Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, for the sake of swift pacification, [I offer] *hrīṃ kroṃ*—bring all people under my control, *svāhā sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ*. *Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ*.
*klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gu gurīṃ ke ī lahrīṃ ha sa ka ha lahrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* We worship Tryambaka, the sweet-smelling, the increaser of prosperity.
May he deliver me from death as a cucumber is released from its stalk, [but not] from immortality.
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gu gurīṃ ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la | Gaṃ kṣipra-prasādanāya gaṇapataye vara-varada hrīṃ kroṃ sarva-janaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ || 1 ||

Hrīṃ sakala hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects. Gaṃ, for the sake of swift propitiation, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons: Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ sarva.
Bring people under my control, svāhā! Sauṃ klīṃ aiṃ.
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gu gurīṃ ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauṃḥ. Whatever it may be, O slayer of Vṛtra, bring it forth!

Obeisance to Gaṇapati, who brings all people under one's control, who is swift in granting grace, the bestower of boons; *hrīṃ kroṃ*, bring all people into my power, *svāhā*! *sauṃḥ klīṃ aiṃ*. *oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ*.

*klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gu gurīṃ ke ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* By this verse, "We have conquered today; we are sinless before Āsana," may [the Lord] protect us from that which arises in dreams and mental constructs— the enemy whom we hate.
May he not encounter distress from those two;
O Gaṅgā, O Gaṇapati, swift-gracious one, bestower of boons, ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ, bring all people under my control, SVĀHĀ SAUṂ KLĪṂ AIṂ. OṂ BHŪR BHUVAḤ SVAḤ ŚA.
There was no place for the two-footed or the four-footed. Oṃ hrīṃ vaṃ ṭhaṃ! O Amṛtarudra, āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ!
May that which is unfavorable to me perish; bring that which is favorable to me under my control, svāhā! [And] by means of Damayantī and Nala.
I offer my salutation so that there may be freedom from dispute,
the pacification of the faults of the Kali age, and so that these Brahmins of diverse intellects may attain unanimity and that concord may arise through dialogue.

Having recited "Niprasīdame" for the fourth time, [one should say]: "O Lord of Devas, accept this state of being a lineage-holder of the most secret of secrets; may there be accomplishment through your grace for this recitation performed by us."
"One should offer the recitation (japa) to Maheśvara"— thus is the application of the *Vāñchākalpalatā* extracted from the root text by the son of Vrajarāja, O King, through his own intelligence.
Having thoroughly reflected upon the Atharvaṇa known as the Gaparijāta and having also deliberated upon the Kumārasaṃhitā, it was indeed proclaimed;
thus has the Saṃkalpalatā-vidyā been fully described.

This should be meditated upon by groups of wise men free from envy for the sake of accomplishing their desired goals. [Thus ends the ritual application for the propitiation of the Wish-Fulfilling Creeper of Śrī Tripurasundarī. By chance... [the text breaks off].
Even if one has drunk water for only a single day, or even through fasting, one must perform one hundred and eight repetitions of the Kalpalatā mantra;
this alone constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Thus...
If one recites this four times every day at the end of the night, all prosperity shall arise;
one attains the fruit of all the Vedāntas. Thus, may there be auspiciousness! || || ||
The Hymn to Gaṇeśa, the Destroyer of Peril.

Nārada said: Having bowed one’s head to the God, the son of Gaurī, who is accompanied by Vināyaka, one should constantly remember Him, the abode of devotion, for the sake of attaining long life, desire, and wealth.
First is Ekavaktra, and Ekadanta is the second.
The third has black and tawny eyes, and the fourth has the face of an elephant.
The fifth is Lambodara, and the sixth is Vikaṭa.
The seventh is Vighnarāja, and the eighth is likewise smoke-colored.
The ninth is Bhālacaṇḍa, and the tenth is Vināyaka.
The eleventh is Gaṇapati, and the twelfth is Gajānana.
The man who recites these twelve names at the three junctions of the day [attains the supreme goal].
He has no fear of obstacles; this is the supreme means for accomplishing all siddhis.
One who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge; one who seeks wealth obtains wealth.
One desiring sons obtains sons; one desiring liberation attains the goal.
One should recite the Gaṇapati-stotra; within six months one shall obtain the fruit, or within a year one attains perfection—of this there is no doubt.
Whoever, having transcribed these eight [verses] of the Brāhmaṇas, should offer them, shall obtain all knowledge through the grace of Gaṇeśa.
[Thus ends the hymn to Gaṇeśa named "The Destroyer of Difficulties" in the glorious Nārada Purāṇa.]
